questions.question: A table ORDERS(order_id PK, customer_id FK, product_id FK, quantity, price) has no index on customer_id. Which execution plan change occurs when you add an index on customer_id and run: SELECT * FROM ORDERS WHERE customer_id = 101 ORDER BY price DESC?
options: Full table scan replaced by index range scan; filesort still required on price
Full table scan replaced by index range scan; ORDER BY is automatically optimized away
Index is ignored because ORDER BY uses a non-indexed column
MySQL uses the index for ORDER BY price but ignores it for the WHERE clause
questions.answer: Full table scan replaced by index range scan; filesort still required on price

questions.question:
Consider the following MySQL snippet:
What is the net effect on the database?
snippetLines: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE id = 2;
options: Account 1 loses 500; account 2 is unchanged; COMMIT persists this state
Both updates are rolled back; no change is committed
Account 1 loses 500 and account 2 gains 500; both are committed
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT rolls back the entire transaction before COMMIT
questions.answer: Account 1 loses 500; account 2 is unchanged; COMMIT persists this state

questions.question:
Given the schema below, which query correctly lists department names that have MORE than 2 employees earning above 50000?

Schema:
- DEPT(dept_id PK, dept_name)
- EMP(emp_id PK, emp_name, salary, dept_id FK)

diagramData.representation: DEPT(dept_id PK, dept_name) | EMP(emp_id PK, emp_name, salary, dept_id FK -> DEPT.dept_id)

options: SELECT d.dept_name FROM DEPT d JOIN EMP e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id WHERE e.salary > 50000 GROUP BY d.dept_name HAVING COUNT(*) > 2
SELECT dept_name FROM DEPT WHERE dept_id IN (SELECT dept_id FROM EMP WHERE salary > 50000 HAVING COUNT(*) > 2)
SELECT d.dept_name FROM DEPT d JOIN EMP e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id GROUP BY d.dept_name HAVING COUNT(e.salary > 50000) > 2
SELECT dept_name FROM DEPT d, EMP e WHERE d.dept_id = e.dept_id AND salary > 50000 HAVING COUNT(*) > 2
questions.answer: SELECT d.dept_name FROM DEPT d JOIN EMP e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id WHERE e.salary > 50000 GROUP BY d.dept_name HAVING COUNT(*) > 2

questions.question: A relation R(A, B, C, D) has functional dependencies: A→B, B→C, A→D. Which normal form is R in, and what decomposition achieves 3NF?
options: R is in 2NF; decompose into R1(A,B,D) and R2(B,C) to achieve 3NF
R is in 1NF; decompose into R1(A,B) and R2(B,C,D) to achieve 3NF
R is in 3NF already because A is the primary key
R is in 2NF; decompose into R1(A,C,D) and R2(A,B) to achieve 3NF
questions.answer: R is in 2NF; decompose into R1(A,B,D) and R2(B,C) to achieve 3NF

questions.question: Examine the MongoDB query below. What does it return from a 'products' collection?
options: Documents with price > 100 in Electronics or Gadgets categories, returning only name and price fields
Documents with price >= 100 in Electronics and Gadgets categories, returning all fields except _id
Documents with price > 100 in Electronics or Gadgets categories, returning all fields
Documents with price > 100 only in Electronics category, returning name and price
questions.answer: Documents with price > 100 in Electronics or Gadgets categories, returning only name and price fields

options: Bob

questions.question: In MySQL InnoDB, which isolation level prevents dirty reads and non-repeatable reads but still allows phantom reads?
options: REPEATABLE READ
READ COMMITTED
SERIALIZABLE
READ UNCOMMITTED
questions.answer: REPEATABLE READ

snippetLines: SELECT COUNT(*) INTO cnt FROM EMP WHERE dept_id = 10;
options: NULL

questions.question: Which of Codd's 12 rules states that every value in a relational database must be accessible by specifying the table name, primary key value, and column name?
options: Rule 2: Guaranteed Access Rule
Rule 1: Information Rule
Rule 6: View Updating Rule
Rule 3: Systematic Treatment of NULL Values
questions.answer: Rule 2: Guaranteed Access Rule

questions.question: Given the ERD below, CUSTOMER(cust_id PK, name) has a one-to-many relationship with ORDERS(order_id PK, cust_id FK, amount). Which query finds customers who have placed NO orders?

diagramData.representation: CUSTOMER(cust_id PK, name) ---[1]---<places>---[M]--- ORDERS(order_id PK, cust_id FK, amount)

options: SELECT c.name FROM CUSTOMER c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ORDERS o WHERE o.cust_id = c.cust_id)
SELECT c.name FROM CUSTOMER c LEFT JOIN ORDERS o ON c.cust_id = o.cust_id WHERE o.amount IS NULL
SELECT c.name FROM CUSTOMER c WHERE c.cust_id NOT IN (SELECT cust_id FROM ORDERS WHERE cust_id IS NOT NULL)
All of the above are equivalent and correct
questions.answer: All of the above are equivalent and correct

questions.question: A BEFORE INSERT trigger is defined on table PRODUCT to set a default category if NULL. A user runs: INSERT INTO PRODUCT(prod_id, name, category) VALUES (10, 'Pen', NULL). What happens?
options: The trigger fires before the row is inserted and can modify NEW.category before it is stored
The trigger fires after the row is inserted; the NULL is stored first, then updated
BEFORE triggers cannot modify column values in MySQL
The INSERT fails because category is NULL and triggers cannot override constraints
questions.answer: The trigger fires before the row is inserted and can modify NEW.category before it is stored

questions.question: Evaluate the following MongoDB aggregation pipeline. What does it produce from a 'sales' collection with fields: {item, qty, price}?
options: Total revenue per item for sales with qty >= 10, sorted by revenue descending
Total revenue per item for all sales, sorted by revenue ascending
Count of items where qty >= 10, grouped by price
Sum of qty per item where price >= 10, sorted descending
questions.answer: Total revenue per item for sales with qty >= 10, sorted by revenue descending

questions.question: A relation is in BCNF if and only if:
options: For every non-trivial functional dependency X→Y, X is a superkey
For every non-trivial functional dependency X→Y, Y is a prime attribute
There are no partial dependencies on the primary key
All multi-valued dependencies are eliminated
questions.answer: For every non-trivial functional dependency X→Y, X is a superkey

options: Raj, Neha

questions.answer: Raj, Neha

questions.question: In the CAP theorem for NoSQL databases, what does it mean when a system chooses AP over CP?
options: The system remains available and partition tolerant but may return stale or inconsistent data
The system is always consistent and partition tolerant but may become unavailable
The system guarantees ACID properties under network partitions
The system rejects writes during partitions to maintain consistency
questions.answer: The system remains available and partition tolerant but may return stale or inconsistent data

questions.question: A cursor is declared in a stored procedure as: DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND SET done = 1. What is the purpose of this handler?
options: It sets done = 1 when the cursor FETCH finds no more rows, allowing the WHILE loop to terminate gracefully
It terminates the stored procedure immediately when no rows are found
It rolls back the current transaction when the cursor is exhausted
It re-opens the cursor from the beginning when all rows are fetched
questions.answer: It sets done = 1 when the cursor FETCH finds no more rows, allowing the WHILE loop to terminate gracefully

questions.question: Which MongoDB update operation increments the 'views' field by 1 and sets 'lastUpdated' to the current date only if the document exists? It should NOT insert a new document.
options: db.articles.updateOne({ title: 'DBT' }, { $inc: { views: 1 }, $set: { lastUpdated: new Date() } })
db.articles.updateOne({ title: 'DBT' }, { $inc: { views: 1 } }, { upsert: true })
db.articles.replaceOne({ title: 'DBT' }, { views: 1, lastUpdated: new Date() })
db.articles.findOneAndUpdate({ title: 'DBT' }, { views: { $inc: 1 } })
questions.answer: db.articles.updateOne({ title: 'DBT' }, { $inc: { views: 1 }, $set: { lastUpdated: new Date() } })

The balance after T1's update (the dirty read)
NULL, because the row is locked by T1
An error is thrown due to the concurrent write

questions.question: A NATURAL JOIN between tables A(id, name, dept_id) and B(dept_id, dept_name) joins on dept_id automatically. If table A has 4 rows and table B has 3 rows, and 2 rows in A have dept_id values not present in B, how many rows does the NATURAL JOIN return?
Which of the following correctly describes a COMPLEX VIEW in MySQL and its limitation?
options: A view based on multiple tables or containing GROUP BY/DISTINCT; it cannot be used for DML operations
A view that uses stored procedures internally; it cannot be queried directly
A view with more than 5 columns; it can only be used for SELECT operations
A view with subqueries in the WHERE clause; it supports INSERT but not UPDATE
questions.answer: A view based on multiple tables or containing GROUP BY/DISTINCT; it cannot be used for DML operations

questions.question:
Consider the following schema:

PROJECT(proj_id PK, proj_name, budget)
ASSIGNMENT(emp_id FK, proj_id FK, hours) — composite PK(emp_id, proj_id)
EMPLOYEE(emp_id PK, name, skill)

Which query finds employees assigned to ALL projects with budget > 100000?

diagramData.representation: PROJECT(proj_id PK, proj_name, budget) | ASSIGNMENT(emp_id FK->EMPLOYEE, proj_id FK->PROJECT, hours) PK(emp_id,proj_id) | EMPLOYEE(emp_id PK, name, skill)

options: SELECT e.name FROM EMPLOYEE e WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT p.proj_id FROM PROJECT p WHERE p.budget > 100000 AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ASSIGNMENT a WHERE a.emp_id = e.emp_id AND a.proj_id = p.proj_id))

SELECT e.name FROM EMPLOYEE e JOIN ASSIGNMENT a ON e.emp_id = a.emp_id JOIN PROJECT p ON a.proj_id = p.proj_id WHERE p.budget > 100000 GROUP BY e.name HAVING COUNT(*) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM PROJECT WHERE budget > 100000)
Both A and B are correct approaches
SELECT e.name FROM EMPLOYEE e WHERE e.emp_id IN (SELECT emp_id FROM ASSIGNMENT WHERE proj_id IN (SELECT proj_id FROM PROJECT WHERE budget > 100000))
questions.answer: Both A and B are correct approaches

questions.question: What is the key difference between MyISAM and InnoDB storage engines in MySQL regarding transactions?
options: InnoDB supports ACID-compliant transactions with row-level locking; MyISAM does not support transactions and uses table-level locking
MyISAM supports transactions with MVCC; InnoDB uses table-level locking only
Both support transactions but InnoDB is faster for read-heavy workloads
MyISAM supports foreign keys; InnoDB does not
questions.answer: InnoDB supports ACID-compliant transactions with row-level locking; MyISAM does not support transactions and uses table-level locking

options: cid=101 total=500; cid=103 total=400
cid=101 total=500 only
cid=103 total=400 only
cid=101 total=500; cid=102 total=150; cid=103 total=400
questions.answer: cid=101 total=500; cid=103 total=400

questions.question: A developer GRANTs SELECT on a view V to user U with GRANT OPTION. User U then grants SELECT on V to user W. The DBA then REVOKES SELECT on V from U with CASCADE. What happens to W's privilege?
options: W's SELECT privilege on V is also revoked due to CASCADE
W retains the privilege because it was granted by U, not the DBA
W's privilege is converted to a direct privilege from DBA
CASCADE only affects the privilege of U; W is unaffected
questions.answer: W's SELECT privilege on V is also revoked due to CASCADE

questions.question: Which MongoDB query deletes ALL documents in the 'logs' collection where 'status' is 'expired' AND 'age' is greater than 30?
options: db.logs.deleteMany({ status: 'expired', age: { $gt: 30 } })
db.logs.deleteOne({ status: 'expired', age: { $gt: 30 } })
db.logs.remove({ $and: [{ status: 'expired' }, { age: { $gte: 30 } }] })
db.logs.drop({ status: 'expired', age: { $gt: 30 } })
questions.answer: db.logs.deleteMany({ status: 'expired', age: { $gt: 30 } })

questions.question: A relation R(A, B, C) where A→B and B→A (A and B are mutually dependent) and B→C. The candidate keys are {A} and {B}. Is this relation in BCNF?
options: Yes, because every non-trivial FD has a superkey on the left side (A and B are both superkeys)
No, because B→C violates BCNF since B is not a superkey
No, because A→B creates a partial dependency
Yes, but only if C is a prime attribute
questions.answer: Yes, because every non-trivial FD has a superkey on the left side (A and B are both superkeys)

questions.question: An e-commerce application needs to find products that exist in the INVENTORY table but have NEVER appeared in any ORDER_ITEMS row. Which approach is most efficient with large tables and why?
options: NOT EXISTS subquery, because it short-circuits as soon as a matching row is found
LEFT JOIN with IS NULL check on the joined table's key
NOT IN with a subquery on ORDER_ITEMS
Both NOT EXISTS and LEFT JOIN are equally efficient; NOT IN may fail if ORDER_ITEMS has NULL values in the join column
questions.answer: Both NOT EXISTS and LEFT JOIN are equally efficient; NOT IN may fail if ORDER_ITEMS has NULL values in the join column

IF base_sal > 80000 THEN SET bonus = base_sal * 0.20;

questions.question: In MongoDB, what is the difference between $set and $replace (replaceOne) when updating a document?
options: $set updates only the specified fields while preserving others; replaceOne replaces the entire document except _id
$set replaces the entire document; replaceOne updates only specified fields
Both $set and replaceOne replace the entire document
$set inserts a new document if none matches; replaceOne never inserts
questions.answer: $set updates only the specified fields while preserving others; replaceOne replaces the entire document except _id

questions.question: A hospital database has: PATIENT(pid PK, name, ward_id FK), WARD(ward_id PK, ward_name, capacity). A report is needed showing wards with more patients than their capacity. Which query is correct?

diagramData.representation: PATIENT(pid PK, name, ward_id FK -> WARD.ward_id) | WARD(ward_id PK, ward_name, capacity INT)

options: SELECT w.ward_name FROM WARD w JOIN PATIENT p ON w.ward_id = p.ward_id GROUP BY w.ward_id, w.ward_name, w.capacity HAVING COUNT(p.pid) > w.capacity
SELECT ward_name FROM WARD WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM PATIENT WHERE ward_id = WARD.ward_id) > capacity
Both A and B produce the correct result
SELECT ward_name FROM WARD w, PATIENT p WHERE w.ward_id = p.ward_id AND COUNT(*) > capacity
questions.answer: Both A and B produce the correct result

questions.question: Which type of index in MySQL would be MOST beneficial for a column 'email' that must be unique and is frequently searched with exact match (=) queries?
options: UNIQUE index, because it enforces uniqueness and creates a B-tree for O(log n) lookups
FULLTEXT index, because email contains text and needs pattern matching
COMPOSITE index on (email, id), because it covers both lookup and key access
SPATIAL index, because email data is high-cardinality
questions.answer: UNIQUE index, because it enforces uniqueness and creates a B-tree for O(log n) lookups

questions.question: An AFTER UPDATE trigger on SALARY_HISTORY records old and new salaries. An employee's salary is updated from 50000 to 65000. Which values do OLD and NEW hold inside the trigger body?
options: OLD.salary = 50000; NEW.salary = 65000
OLD.salary = 65000; NEW.salary = 50000
OLD.salary = NULL; NEW.salary = 65000
OLD and NEW are both 65000 after the update commits
questions.answer: OLD.salary = 50000; NEW.salary = 65000

questions.question: A table PRODUCT(prod_id PK AUTO_INCREMENT, name, price) has rows 1–5. After DELETE FROM PRODUCT WHERE prod_id = 5 and INSERT INTO PRODUCT(name, price) VALUES('Pen', 10), what is the prod_id of 'Pen'?
options: 6, because AUTO_INCREMENT continues from the highest ever used value, not the current max
5, because the last deleted ID is reused
1, because AUTO_INCREMENT resets after a delete
NULL, because AUTO_INCREMENT fails after a delete
questions.answer: 6, because AUTO_INCREMENT continues from the highest ever used value, not the current max

questions.question: In a MongoDB collection 'students', each document has an embedded array 'scores'. Which query returns students who have AT LEAST ONE score greater than 90?
options: db.students.find({ scores: { $gt: 90 } })
db.students.find({ scores: { $elemMatch: { $gt: 90 } } })
db.students.find({ 'scores.$': { $gt: 90 } })
db.students.find({ scores: { $all: [{ $gt: 90 }] } })
questions.answer: db.students.find({ scores: { $elemMatch: { $gt: 90 } } })

questions.question: Consider a scenario where a college keeps STUDENT(sid, sname, dept_id, dept_name, hod_name). The dependency chain is: sid→dept_id, dept_id→dept_name, dept_id→hod_name. This table suffers from which specific anomaly if a department's HOD changes?
options: Update anomaly: the HOD name must be changed in every student row belonging to that department
Insertion anomaly: a new department cannot be added without at least one student
Deletion anomaly: deleting all students in a department removes department information
All three anomalies are present due to transitive dependency
questions.answer: All three anomalies are present due to transitive dependency

options: NULL

questions.question: In the BASE model used by NoSQL databases, what does 'Eventually Consistent' mean?
options: The system guarantees that all nodes will converge to the same value given sufficient time without new updates
The system is immediately consistent after every write operation
The system rejects reads until all replicas are synchronized
The system uses distributed transactions to maintain consistency
questions.answer: The system guarantees that all nodes will converge to the same value given sufficient time without new updates

questions.question: A library system uses: BOOK(isbn PK, title, author_id FK), AUTHOR(author_id PK, name, country). The manager wants names of authors who have written MORE than 3 books AND are from 'India'. Which query is correct?

diagramData.representation: BOOK(isbn PK, title, author_id FK -> AUTHOR.author_id) | AUTHOR(author_id PK, name, country)

options: SELECT a.name FROM AUTHOR a JOIN BOOK b ON a.author_id = b.author_id WHERE a.country = 'India' GROUP BY a.author_id, a.name HAVING COUNT(b.isbn) > 3
SELECT name FROM AUTHOR WHERE country = 'India' AND author_id IN (SELECT author_id FROM BOOK GROUP BY author_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 3)
Both A and B are correct
SELECT a.name FROM AUTHOR a, BOOK b WHERE a.author_id = b.author_id AND a.country = 'India' HAVING COUNT(*) > 3
questions.answer: Both A and B are correct

questions.question: A WHILE loop in a MySQL stored procedure iterates over cursor rows. The loop condition checks 'done = 0'. The NOT FOUND handler sets done = 1. What happens if the table queried by the cursor is empty?
options: The first FETCH immediately triggers NOT FOUND, sets done = 1, and the WHILE loop never executes its body
The procedure throws an error because a cursor cannot be opened on an empty table
The WHILE loop executes once with NULL values before the handler fires
done remains 0 and the loop runs indefinitely
questions.answer: The first FETCH immediately triggers NOT FOUND, sets done = 1, and the WHILE loop never executes its body

questions.question:
A relational table FLIGHT(flight_no, from_city, to_city, departure_time, airline) has the following FDs:
flight_no → airline, from_city, to_city
(from_city, to_city, departure_time) → flight_no
What are the candidate keys of this relation?
options: {flight_no} and {from_city, to_city, departure_time}
{flight_no} only
{airline, departure_time} and {flight_no}
{from_city, to_city, departure_time, airline}
questions.answer: {flight_no} and {from_city, to_city, departure_time}
